SEWAGE IRRIGATION. 
TO THE EDITOR OF THE INDIAN MEDICAL GAZETTE. 
Sib,?An article in the Saturday Review of the 19th Octo- 
ber last gives the latest information on the progress of sewage 
irrigation in England, and more particularly on the success of 
the '? sewage farm at Romford."' 
I had intended to put together notes on a- visit to the above 
farm for the information of your readers, and to the camp farm 
at Aldershot, inspected during the summer of 1871 : 
but other 
matters have occupied my time; and the successful progress 
at Romford, as detailed in the Saturday Review, would render 
my notes almost out of date ; I shall therefore content myself 
with drawing attention to the excellent article in question, and 
penning a few lines on the applicability of the system, which 
lias proved so successful at Romford, to India. 
I have always 
held the opinion that where water can be had in sufficient 
quantity, &c., it is the most efficient agent for the removal of 
sewage. Sanitary science in England is also yearly recog- 
nizing it as the best agent for the utilization of sewage. 
The progress of knowledge on the subject in England has 
now reached that stage that it may be safely asserted that the 
test plan for the disposal and utilization of sewage is to bring 
water in, to convey it out laden with sewage matters, and to 
apply such sewage to cultivation. 
The success which has 
attended the operation of this system in Calcutta should make 
us think in India how it may be further extended for the benefit 
of other Indian communities. 
It is almost needless to state the fact that there is not one 
station in the Bengal Presidency?away from Calcutta?one 
barrack latrine, or one homestead, in which the disposal of 
sewage is accomplished in a manner which may be considered 
sanitarily safe. 
As a rule, barrack latrines are in the same foul 
condition as they were ten years ago 
. and so they will continue 
until an efficient carrier-off of sewage is provided. 
At once then to come to the p >int?why not use our great 
rivers for the disposal of sewage and for its utilization ? Many 
of our largest stations are situated on the banks of rivers, 
surrounded by a sandy country or poor lands. 
Water might 
be brought in from up stream, conducted through the station, 
washing everything before it, and let out beyond it to bo 
distributed upon land which it would soon fertilize, and in all 
probability ttie profits thus realized would pay the interest, at 
least, of the capital expended upon the necessary works and 
provide for current outlay. 
I am aware that this is a very large subject, involving a mass 
of questions, opinions, and details, which I have not leisure to 
sift or examine: but I merely put forward the idea that tho 
above is a safe, practical, and economical plan for the proper 
disposal of sewage in most stations of the Bengal Presidency. 
I would also urge in support of my proposal, that the supply 
of really good water would constitute an important part of the 
scheme. The water-supply of every city and station in India

(except Calcutta and Bombay) is liable to all kinds of conta- 
minations in all its stages as it passes from the source to the 
consumer. 
I have no hesitation in stating that notwithstanding 
all that has been spoken, written, and done in this matter, the 
subject of water purification and conservancy is still in its 
infancy in India. The system I would strongly urge is to obtain 
a good body of water from an unobjectionable source, to subject 
it to a systematic and thorough process of " settling," aeration 
and filtration, to adapt arrangements by which all the sewage of a 
city or station should be immediately and completely removed 
hy the agency of water, and to utilize this promptly in the way 
of irrigation for the purpose of fertilizing the land. 
No other 
system?not even the dry-earth or the tench system?can com- 
pare with this in simplicity and efficiency. 
It leaves less to the 
discretion of individuals or the labor of costly establishments 
than any other system known, and places at the disposal of all 
a certain and easy, almost self-acting, mechanical agency in 
place of an uncertain and complicated human agency, which i3 
ever liable to shortcoming and error.

I am, &c., 
F. II. C. S.
